content:
One report about a sheep and a sheet of paper has been used for generations to argue that the Quran lost verses. It appears in a canonical collection, and it deserves a full account of its chain and its readers.

The report is popular with critics because it seems to combine three charges in one picture: that verses were kept carelessly, that they were lost by accident, and that the Companions did nothing to recover them. If all three were true, the Muslim claim that the Quran was preserved would be in serious trouble. Each depends on reading the report in a particular way, and the hadith scholars who first examined it read it differently.

The five points below take the report, the way it was transmitted, the criticism of its narrator, the disagreement over its grade and the replies of Ibn Hazm and al-Baqillani.

Critics quote a report in Sunan Ibn Majah. A'isha said that the verse of stoning and of suckling an adult ten times was revealed, that it was written on a paper kept under her pillow, and that a tame sheep came in and ate it after the Prophet died.[1] The conclusion drawn is that verses of the Quran were lost, and that the claim of a preserved book fails.

The same A'isha is also reported in Sahih Muslim as saying that the Quran once stated ten known sucklings make marriage unlawful, that this was replaced by five known sucklings, and that the earlier wording was still being recited when the Prophet died.[2] Her own words describe a ruling that was changed, which is a different thing from a chapter that disappeared.

Muslim scholars had a name for what she describes: abrogation of the recitation, in which a verse is withdrawn from the text of the Quran while, in some cases, its ruling remains. The Quran speaks of God abrogating a verse or causing it to be forgotten and bringing one better or like it, and of the Prophet being made to recite so that he will not forget, "except what God wills".[3] Al-Suyuti set out the three classical categories: a verse whose wording and ruling are both withdrawn, as with the ten sucklings; a verse whose wording is withdrawn while its ruling stays, as with stoning; and a verse whose wording stays while its ruling is replaced.[4]

The phrase "still being recited when the Prophet died" puzzled readers too. Al-Nawawi explained it in his commentary on Sahih Muslim: the abrogation of the five sucklings in recitation came so late that some people had not heard of it and went on reciting the verse, and when the news reached them they stopped and agreed that it was no longer to be recited.[5] The report describes a change completed at the very end of the revelation, which is why it left traces in the memories of a few.

Every version of the report traces back to A'isha through Abdullah ibn Abi Bakr ibn Hazm and Amra bint Abd al-Rahman. Yahya ibn Sa'id al-Ansari, whose version is in Sahih Muslim, and Malik, in the Muwatta', both leave out the sheep. The version of al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, narrated by al-Tahawi, leaves it out as well. Only Muhammad ibn Ishaq includes it, and his version is the one in Ahmad's Musnad and Ibn Majah.[6]

A story that three other narrators from the same source do not mention, and that appears in a single line of transmission, is an exception in the record, which is how the hadith scholars treated it.

The hadith scholars had a technical term for exactly this situation. A detail added by one narrator, which the other narrators from the same source omit, is called an addition (ziyada). If the narrator who adds it is less reliable than those who leave it out, and the addition changes the meaning, the report is classed as irregular (shadhdh), and the addition is not accepted.[7] The sheep is an addition of this kind. Yahya ibn Sa'id and Malik are among the most trusted narrators of Medina, and they report A'isha's words without it.

The strongest form of the objection says that silence proves nothing: other narrators may simply have shortened the story. That happens, and the scholars allowed for it. They also noticed what the sheep adds. Without it, the report is a statement about abrogation. With it, it becomes a story about loss. A detail that turns a report into its opposite needs a stronger witness than a single narrator of disputed standing.

Ibn Hajar's entry on Ibn Ishaq in Tahdhib al-Tahdhib records a mixed verdict, and the mixture matters. His admirers include Shu'ba, who called him the commander of the faithful in hadith, and Ali ibn al-Madini, who judged his hadith sound. The critics include Ahmad ibn Hanbal, who is reported to have said that Ibn Ishaq is not a proof (hujja) and, in the report of his son Abdullah, that he was not cited as proof in matters of the sunan, the legal reports. Yahya ibn Ma'in is reported on both sides: trustworthy but not a proof, and in one report weak. Al-Nasa'i said that he is not strong.[8] The criticism therefore bears most on a report such as this one, which is used to settle a question of law and of the Quran's text.

The editors of Ahmad's Musnad state that the chain is weak because Ibn Ishaq alone narrated it.[9] Ibn Qutayba went further in the third century of the Hijra. He judged the report of adult suckling ten times to be a mistake of Ibn Ishaq, observed that Malik narrated the same hadith from Abdullah ibn Abi Bakr with different wording, and added that Malik is the more reliable of the two in the view of the hadith scholars.[10] The principle applied is that an odd report from a narrator of disputed strength, which differs from the more reliable narrators, is set aside.

Ibn Ishaq's reputation explains the pattern. He was the great collector of the Prophet's biography, and the critics who doubted his legal reports praised his knowledge of the campaigns and the history. They were more cautious when he alone transmitted a ruling, and when he did not state plainly that he had heard a report from his source, since he was known to pass on reports without naming every link.[8] A narrator can be indispensable in one field and insufficient as sole proof in another, and the classical verdicts on Ibn Ishaq draw exactly that line.

Scholars did not all reach the same grading. The page of Ibn Majah 1944 on sunnah.com shows Darussalam's grade of hasan, and the fatwa site Islamweb reports that al-Albani graded the report hasan.[1][11] The editors of the Musnad call it weak, and the arguments of the previous point lead several scholars to the same view.[9]

A fair reading states the disagreement. Where the grading is hasan, the argument in the next point answers the objection, and where the grading is weak, the objection never begins.

The difference between the grades is narrower than it looks. A grade of hasan means that a chain meets the conditions for acceptance, with a narrator whose precision falls a little short of the highest level. Scholars who grade the chain hasan still have to ask whether each detail of the wording is secure, and whether it agrees with the stronger versions. The question of the sheep can be answered on its own terms, whichever grade a reader prefers.

The strongest form of the objection holds that even a hasan report shows something of the Quran was lost, since the verses are no longer in the book. That is the point the last entry addresses. Whether the verses were lost depends on whether they were still part of the Quran when the sheet was eaten, and on that question the report and its readers give a clear answer.

Ibn Hazm quoted the report with its chain and wrote that it is sound, but not in the sense the objectors take. The verse of stoning was memorised and acted on by the Prophet, but the scribes of the Quran did not write it in the codex, so its wording was abrogated, and the sheet that held it was no loss. The same holds for the verse on suckling. If the verses had still been part of the Quran, he argued, the eating of the sheet would not have prevented the Companions from writing them down from memory.[12]

Al-Baqillani dealt with the report in his book defending the Quran. He wrote that the Prophet reviewed the Quran each year, and twice in the year he died, and that the Companions and scribes were appointed to preserve it, so it is not conceivable that a verse of the Book was kept only on a sheet under A'isha's bed, where a household animal could eat it, while no one else remembered it.[13] The Quran's text rested on the community. The stoning ruling rests on the practice of the Prophet and his successors, as the previous article sets out.[14]

Other reports confirm that the stoning verse was known and discussed apart from any sheet. Umar ibn al-Khattab said from the pulpit that God had revealed the verse of stoning, that the Companions had recited it and understood it, and that the Prophet had applied the penalty; he feared that people would later deny the ruling because they could not find it in the Book.[14] Umar speaks of a verse that people knew and a ruling that remained, which is the category al-Suyuti describes, and he does not suggest that a verse still in the Quran had been lost.

The strongest modern objection comes from scholars who doubt the whole theory of abrogated recitation. John Burton argued that the jurists developed it to reconcile legal practice with the text of the Quran.[15] Some Muslim scholars, past and present, have also rejected the category. That debate is real, and it concerns how the law was derived. It does not revive the picture of a lost verse, because on either view the Companions, who knew the verses by heart, did not include them in the written Quran. The sheet was not the only place they existed.

The bottom line

The sheep appears in one line of transmission, through a narrator whom the critics trusted for history and doubted for law, and the more reliable narrators of the same report leave it out. Scholars disagree about the grade of that version, and the argument does not depend on settling the disagreement. On A'isha's own words in Sahih Muslim, the verses on suckling were abrogated by the time of the Prophet's death, and on the reports of Umar, the stoning ruling remained while its verse was withdrawn.

Ibn Hazm and al-Baqillani gave the decisive answer centuries ago. A verse that was still part of the Quran could not have disappeared with a sheet of paper, because the Quran was held in the memories of the Companions and recited in full before the Prophet each year. A household animal could eat a page. It could not remove a verse from the community that recited it.

  3. Quran 2:106; 87:6–7.

  5. Al-Nawawi, al-Minhaj Sharh Sahih Muslim, commentary on Sahih Muslim 1452, Book of Suckling.
